wa_north_face_left_buttress.notes: Cross the moat and start in the blocky line of face holds just left of the gully/chimney that bounds the left edge of the buttress. Most of the pitch is low fifth class on clean granite; a wide crack near the top holds the harder moves. The moat at the start can be awkward and changes through the season.

Trend up and right to the top of the lingering snow patch, aiming for the clean wall beneath a shallow left-facing corner. How much snow sits here varies a lot year to year, and in a big year it can bury this ground; belay at the base of the clean wall.

Unprotected but balancy face climbing leads to the corner, which takes good gear and has had a fixed piton in it. Above the top of the crack, hard face climbing on good gear finishes at a belay ledge. The runout off the belay comes before the first solid piece, so move carefully.

Face climb left off the belay on positive holds with little protection, then pull into a steep dihedral split by twin cracks and follow clean flakes and cracks to a pedestal. Among the best pitches on the route; gear is mostly small.

Step down and left from the belay into a hidden corner, climb it, and work back up and right to belay at a spot directly above the previous stance. The corner is not visible from the pedestal, so traverse down to find it rather than forcing straight up.

Move left and up to the base of a long seam and finger crack, which protects well as the moves get harder. From its base work left and up around a series of left-facing corners and small roofs toward the left edge of the wall, belaying low beside the chimney/gully.

Climb the featured arête right of the chimney/gully, then a clean white shallow dihedral, and undercling right to the belay. Protection on the arête is sparse and relies on small cams (TCU sizes); expect a long, committing stretch that some find runout.

A strenuous left-facing corner with sustained finger locks leads on up the left side of the buttress. Above this pitch the rock turns noticeably mossier, especially in the obvious dihedrals, so avoid the corners and look for cleaner flakes and cracks.

Follow flakes and cracks left onto a bright quartz dike, which gives about two pitches of continuous positive holds with only occasional gear. From a small ledge below the summit, a hidden snow patch and a steep final rock wall with an overhanging pull-up move lead to the top; an ice tool helps if that snow is still there.

wa_himmelhorn_stonehenge.notes: Starts from the grassy col, where the rope and rack come out after the long ramp-and-ledge scramble from the snow. Blocky terrain makes for straightforward climbing to the first belay.
The crux. A dihedral looks like the natural line but dead-ends, so the leader steps left onto the open face and finishes up a hand crack.
Quite easy ground that connects the hard pitches below to the steeper climbing above.
A steep flake of good quality gives the climbing on this pitch.
A rightward traverse leads to the foot of the summit tower. No grade is recorded for it.
A steep face about two-thirds of the way up the tower. It is run out, so expect little protection between the holds.

A moderate rightward traverse that feels wild and exposed, on solid rock with almost nothing to protect it. It ends in the notch between the summit tower and a neighbouring pinnacle, which marks the end of the difficulties.
One easy but loose pitch from the notch to the summit; test blocks before weighting them.
